items.title: Maktaba Ndogo ya Darasa la Tano
items.body:
Jana asubuhi, mwalimu wetu Bi. Wanjiku aliingia darasani akiwa na tabasamu kubwa. Alituambia kwamba shule yetu itafungua maktaba ndogo karibu na uwanja, chini ya mti mkubwa. Kila darasa liliombwa kuchagua vitabu na kuvipanga vizuri kwenye rafu.

Mimi na rafiki yangu Zawadi tulipewa kazi ya kuandika majina ya vitabu kwenye karatasi za rangi tofauti. Tuliketi kivulini, tukafungua sanduku la vitabu vya hadithi. Kulikuwa na kitabu kuhusu ndege, kingine kuhusu bustani, na kingine chenye picha za milima ya Kenya.

"Tuanze na vitabu vya hadithi," alisema Zawadi, "kwa sababu watoto wadogo hupenda kusikiliza." Tulikubaliana. Kila kitabu kilipewa nambari na kuwekwa kwenye rafu yake. Vitabu virefu viliwekwa kwenye rafu ya chini, na vifupi viliwekwa kwenye rafu ya juu ili visianguke.

Wakati wa mapumziko, watoto wa darasa la kwanza walikuja. Mmoja wao, aitwaye Otieno, alichagua kitabu chenye picha ya twiga. Aliniomba nimsomee ukurasa wa kwanza. Nilisoma polepole, nikitamka kila neno wazi. Otieno alicheka aliposikia jinsi twiga inavyoinamisha shingo ili kula majani laini.

Bi. Wanjiku alipita na kutusifu. "Maktaba si jengo tu," alisema. "Ni mahali pa kukutana na hadithi." Maneno hayo yalibaki kichwani mwangu.

Alasiri, tuliweka godoro dogo kwenye kiti cha kusomea. Kisha tukaandika tangazo: "Karibu. Chukua kitabu, usome, kisha urudishe." Kabla hatujaondoka, niliweka kitabu nilichokipenda zaidi kwenye rafu ya kwanza. Kesho nitamwalika mdogo wangu aje aone maktaba yetu ndogo.

questions.prompt: Vitabu virefu viliwekwa kwenye rafu gani?
Neno "rafu" linamaanisha nini katika habari hii?
Otieno alichagua kitabu chenye picha ya nini?
"Mapumziko" katika habari hii ni wakati gani?
choices: Wakati wa kupumzika shuleni kati ya masomo

questions.prompt: Bi. Wanjiku alisema maktaba si jengo tu. Ni nini basi?
questions.answer: Ni mahali pa kukutana na hadithi.

items.title: The Kite That Climbed the Clouds
items.body:
On a windy Saturday, Amina and her brother Jabari carried a homemade kite to the open field behind their flat. The kite was made from a black bin liner, four thin sticks, and a long ball of string from the duka. It was not pretty, but it was theirs.

Amina held the string while Jabari ran with the kite. The first time, it flopped onto the grass like a tired fish. The second time, it lifted a little and then dived straight back down. "Again," said Amina, and she checked that the two long sticks crossed in the middle, tightly tied with the string.

On the third try the wind caught the bin liner and pulled. Up went the kite, higher than the water tank on the roof. Jabari shouted and ran in circles. A woman selling mandazi from a cart stopped to watch, and even she clapped.

Soon the kite was a small dark diamond against the wide grey sky. Amina let out more string, little by little, the way her grandmother had taught her. When you give the wind a little, she had said, it gives you a lot. Amina remembered those words and smiled.

Then the wind dropped. The kite wobbled. Amina pulled the string gently, twice, and the kite steadied itself. She learned something that afternoon. A kite is not a thing you hold tightly. It is a thing you talk to.

Her hands were red from the string, so she passed it to Jabari for a while. He held it far too tightly and the kite dived at once. "Gently," said Amina, and she showed him with her own hands how to let it breathe. He tried again, and this time the kite stayed up all by itself, as if it had always known how.

As the sun began to set, they wound the string back and walked home. Their arms ached and their cheeks were dusty, but the kite had flown. "Tomorrow?" asked Jabari. "Tomorrow," said Amina. And she meant it.

items.title: The Missing Chapati
items.body:
Every evening Mama counted the chapatis before she went to the shop, and every evening there were exactly twelve. On Monday evening there were eleven. Mama frowned and counted again, moving her finger over each one like a teacher marking a register.

"Did you eat one, Zawadi?" Mama asked. Zawadi shook her head. Her little brother Otis shook his head too, though the corner of his mouth looked suspiciously shiny, and there was a small crumb sitting on his chin like a tiny pearl.

Zawadi decided to become a detective. She looked under the table. Nothing. She looked in the cupboard. Nothing but a bag of ugali flour and a sleepy cockroach that hurried away when the torch found it. Then she looked behind the curtain, and there sat Otis, with a chapati folded in his lap and the family cat staring at it with great interest.

Zawadi wrote down everything she knew in her exercise book, like a real investigator. The chapati had last been seen on the plate at six o'clock. The suspect list was short. There was Mama, there was herself, there was Otis, and there was the cat, who was pretending to sleep but was watching the plate through one half-open eye.

"Otis," said Zawadi in her most serious voice, "that is stealing." Otis began to cry. The cat took this chance and licked the edge of the chapati. Zawadi tried very hard not to laugh, because detectives do not laugh, but it was difficult.

Mama came back and saw the whole scene. She sighed, and then she laughed properly, from her belly. She cut the chapati into three pieces. One for Otis, one for Zawadi, and one for herself. The cat got the crumbs, and seemed pleased with the arrangement.

"Next time, ask," said Mama. Otis nodded and wiped his eyes. Zawadi found a scrap of paper and wrote a note, which she stuck to the chapati tin. It said, in her best handwriting: DO NOT TOUCH. OTIS.

The next evening there were twelve chapatis, and then, very quickly, there were nine.

items.title: The Rain That Came Late
items.body:
Grandmother's little garden had been waiting for rain for three whole weeks. The soil was pale and cracked, like the back of an old elephant. Every morning Wanjiku carried the small watering can from the tap and gave the seedlings a drink, but the clouds stayed far away over the hills and never moved closer.

"Patience," said Grandmother, as she pulled a dry weed from between the sukuma wiki. "A garden teaches patience even better than it teaches farming." Wanjiku did not think she had time for patience. She wanted tomatoes today, and maybe a carrot as well.

While they waited for the rain, Grandmother taught her the names of the plants. The tall one with yellow flowers was a weed, but a useful one, she said, because it told them the soil was healthy. Wanjiku wrote the names on a stone with a piece of chalk and lined the stones along the path like a tiny classroom.

On Tuesday the sky turned the colour of a bruised plum. Wanjiku ran outside and stood in the middle of the shamba with her arms wide. The first drop hit her nose. The second hit her ear. Then the whole sky opened like a tap, and the rain came down in warm grey sheets.

Grandmother laughed and pulled her under the corrugated iron of the kitchen roof. They watched the water run in little rivers down the path. The sukuma wiki straightened up as though someone had told it good news. The tomato plants drank and drank and drank.

After the rain, everything smelled new. The air was cool and sweet, and the ground squelched under their feet. Wanjiku found three stubborn earthworms on the path and carried each one carefully back to the soil. "They will be good luck," said Grandmother. "They dig the earth for the roots."

That night, Wanjiku wrote in her exercise book: Rain came at last. Garden still alive. Patience is hard but it works. Then she went to sleep listening to the water dripping from the roof, which is one of the nicest sounds in the world.

items.title: The Myna Bird on the Verandah
items.body:
Every morning at half past six, a yellow-eyed myna bird landed on the verandah rail and shouted. It was not singing. It was shouting. The bird seemed to think that the entire estate should be awake by then, and it was doing its best to make sure of it.

Nala named the bird Kofi. She put out a small bowl of water and a few crumbs of bread, then sat very still on the step to watch. Kofi looked at the crumbs, looked at Nala, looked back at the crumbs, and then hopped down with the confidence of a landlord inspecting a new tenant.

Kofi was not a shy bird. It walked along the rail as though the verandah belonged to it and Nala was the visitor. Once it tilted its head and looked straight at her for a long moment, and Nala felt certain it was deciding something important. Then it shook its feathers and screeched at the sky, which Nala took to mean the meeting was over.

By the end of the week, Kofi came even when there was no bread. Nala liked to think the bird came to see her, though her brother said the bird only liked the crumbs. "You do not know that," said Nala. "And neither do you," said her brother, which was annoyingly true.

One morning Kofi arrived with something in its beak. It dropped the thing on the rail and flew off. Nala went to look. It was a shiny bottle cap, and next to it a small blue button. Presents. The bird had brought presents.

Nala kept the button in her pocket and the bottle cap on her windowsill. She told everyone at school that a bird had paid her with a button, and the teacher said that birds build nests with shiny things, so perhaps Kofi was simply moving house.

Nala decided she preferred her own explanation. Some things are better left as small mysteries, like why a bird would ever talk to a girl at half past six in the morning. She put out fresh water, and waited for Kofi to come again.

items.title: Saturday at Gikomba Market
items.body:
Auntie Grace took Chen on a Saturday market trip, and Chen was told to hold on to the edge of her shawl and not let go for anything. The market was a sea of people, colours and noise. Vendors called out prices. A man pushed a handcart piled higher than a giraffe. Somewhere, a radio played dance music.

The first stall had shoes. The second stall had shoes. The third stall also had shoes, and Auntie Grace stopped there. Chen sat on a small wooden stool while the bargaining began. It seemed to take a very long time, and nobody was angry, but both women spoke as though they had been personally insulted by the price.

"Four hundred," said the vendor. "Two hundred," said Auntie Grace. They went back and forth like two birds on a wire. In the end the shoes cost two hundred and fifty shillings, and everyone looked satisfied, which Chen understood was the whole point of the game.

They bought tomatoes, a bundle of greens, and a bag of groundnuts for the walk home. Chen was allowed to pay the groundnut seller by herself. She counted the coins twice, handed them over, and received a warm paper bag in return. She felt extremely important for the rest of the morning.

On the way to the matatu, they passed a woman selling second-hand books on a cloth. Chen found a storybook with a torn cover and a picture of a lion on it. Auntie Grace paid fifty shillings. "Read it tonight," she said. "Then tell me the story."

In the matatu, Chen held the book on her lap and watched the city slide past. Her feet were tired, her head was full of noise, and she was happier than she had been all month. She decided that markets were a kind of library, if you knew where to look.

items.title: The Bottle-Top Race
items.body:
Kamau and Neema stood at the top of the path behind their classroom. Kamau held a red bottle top. Neema held a blue one.

"Ready, go!" said Kamau. The red top rolled into a small stone and stopped. The blue top kept going, all the way past the water tank, and spun in a circle at the bottom.

Neema smiled. "Yours hit the stone. Mine had a clear road." Kamau picked up his top and wiped off the dust. "Again," he said. "This time I will aim away from the stone."

He did. The red top raced past Neema's and clicked against the tank. They laughed so loud that their teacher looked out of the window and smiled.

questions.q: Who had the blue bottle top?
Where did they race?
choices: On the path behind the classroom

questions.q: Why did the red top stop the first time?
Neema told Kamau why his top stopped. Was that a kind thing to do?
What colour was Kamau's bottle top?

items.title: The Blue Jug
items.body:
Before school, Achieng carried the blue jug to the tap. It was big, so she used both hands.

A woman with a baby was first in the queue. Then a boy with a yellow bucket. Achieng waited and hummed the song her class was learning.

When it was her turn, she filled the jug to the top and turned the tap off. Not one drop ran over the side.

On the way home a boda boda came along the path. Achieng stepped to the side and kept the jug steady. At the gate her little brother Otieno ran up. "Is it full?" he asked. Achieng nodded. "Full," she said. "And my shoes are still dry."

items.title: The Ball in the Tree
items.body:
At break, Baraka kicked the football high. It stuck in the branches of the big tree by the fence.

"Throw a stone," said a boy. "No," said Baraka. "A stone can hit someone. It can break a window too."

Mrs Mwangi heard them. She brought a long dry stick and tapped the branch once, gently. The ball dropped into Baraka's hands.

"Thank you," said Baraka. "Next time," said Mrs Mwangi, "kick it along the ground when you are near the tree." Baraka nodded and passed the ball to Juma, low and soft.

questions.q: Where did the ball get stuck?
Why did Baraka say no to throwing a stone?
choices: He wanted to keep the stone

questions.q: Who got the ball down?
How should they kick when they are near the tree?

items.title: Boats in the Rain
items.body:
Rain drummed on the iron roof, so Wanjiku and her cousin Njeri stayed inside. They folded two paper boats from an old exercise-book page.

"Mine is the red one," said Njeri. She coloured the front with a red crayon.

When the rain slowed, Mama looked at the compound. "The ditch by the hedge is shallow," she said. "You may float the boats there. Keep your feet on the grass."

The boats bobbed along. Njeri's boat stuck on a leaf. Wanjiku's boat followed the rainwater all the way to the hedge. Njeri laughed, lifted the leaf off, and tried again. "Best of three?" asked Wanjiku.

questions.q: What did the girls make?
Who said they could float the boats?
Where did Mama tell them to keep their feet?
What stopped Njeri's boat?
What colour did Njeri colour her boat?

items.title: The Blue Matatu
items.body:
Musa held Baba's hand at the stage. Matatus came and went. A green one. A white one. Then a blue one with soft music.

"This one," said Baba. They climbed in. Musa sat by the window and counted the speed bumps. One, two, three.

At the market the air smelled of mangoes. Baba bought four. He gave one to Musa to hold. It was smooth and warm from the sun.

On the way home Musa remembered his manners. "Thank you," he said to the conductor. The conductor smiled. "You are welcome, young man. Enjoy that mango."

questions.q: Who went to the market with Musa?
Which matatu did they ride?
How many speed bumps did Musa count?
What did Baba buy?
What did Musa say to the conductor?
